subject: english-language
topicDisplay: Unit 4 Personal Or Creative Writing And Reading Literary And Non Fiction Texts
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: A third-person narrator who knows the thoughts and feelings of every character is described as:
options: Restricted
Unreliable
First-person
Omniscient
questions.explain: An omniscient narrator has access to all characters' inner thoughts and the wider story.

questions.q: An exam asks: "How does the writer use language to create a sense of fear?" What should your answer focus on?
options: How long the extract is
The author's biography
Specific words and phrases and the effects they create
Retelling the plot of the extract
questions.explain: A "how does the writer use language" question requires analysis of word choices and their effects, not plot summary.

questions.q: To "zoom in" on the quotation "her hands trembled like leaves in a storm," the strongest analytical move is to:
options: Count the number of words
Say it is a nice description
Quote the whole paragraph instead
Comment on the simile and what the comparison suggests about her
questions.explain: Zooming in means analysing the chosen technique (a simile) and the specific impression it gives.

questions.q: Which is an effective way to vary sentence length for tension in narrative writing?
options: Use the same length throughout
Avoid full stops entirely
Use only very long sentences
Follow several longer sentences with a short, punchy one: 'He stopped.'
questions.explain: A sudden short sentence after longer ones creates emphasis and tension.

questions.q: Which sentence is the strongest example of using a metaphor in descriptive writing?
options: The night sky looked like it had stars in it.
The night sky was very dark and a bit cloudy.
The night sky was dark, with some stars showing.
The night sky was a black ocean drowning every star.
questions.explain: Calling the sky 'a black ocean' directly identifies it as something else, creating a vivid metaphor.

questions.q: When a question asks you to track how a writer "builds tension across the extract," you should trace:
options: How tension rises and changes from the beginning through to the end
The title of the chapter
A single quotation only
The number of characters
questions.explain: Tracking tension means following its development across the whole extract, not one moment.

questions.q: Which is the most effective, vivid sensory description of a market?
options: The market was busy and had lots of things.
The market was a place where you could buy stuff.
There were many people at the market buying food.
Spices stung the air, voices clashed overhead, and ripe mangoes glistened on every stall.
questions.explain: It engages multiple senses (smell, sound, sight) to create an immersive image.

questions.q: You are writing a review of a film. Which feature suits the form best?
options: A formal salutation and address block
Stage directions in brackets
A balanced judgement supported by specific examples and a recommendation
A bibliography of academic sources
questions.explain: Reviews give an evaluative judgement backed by examples and end with a recommendation.

questions.q: "The town had not changed, yet nothing felt the same to him now." This sentence mainly invites the reader to focus on:
options: The weather that day
How the character himself has changed inside
The geography of the town
The names of the streets
questions.explain: The contrast between an unchanged town and altered feeling points to internal change in the character.

questions.q: "The letter still lay unopened on the mat, its corner curling in the morning sun." What does the detail of the unopened letter most likely IMPLY?
options: Someone is avoiding or dreading its contents
The letter is unimportant
The character is keen to read it
The postman delivered it late
questions.explain: An unopened, neglected letter implies reluctance or dread rather than eagerness.

questions.q: A narrator describes events plainly with no access to anyone's thoughts, simply reporting what is seen and heard. This perspective is best called:
options: First-person confessional
Objective (dramatic) third-person
Omniscient
Second-person
questions.explain: Reporting only observable action without inner thoughts is an objective third-person perspective.

questions.q: When an extract suddenly shifts focus from a wide view of a crowd to one trembling child, this structural technique:
options: Narrows the focus to direct the reader's attention
Removes all tension
Ends the narrative
Changes the narrator to second person
questions.explain: Moving from the general to a single detail is a deliberate narrowing of focus that guides reader attention.

questions.q: In analysing a fiction extract, the phrase "the effect on the reader" asks you to explain:
options: How the writer's choices make the reader think or feel
The number of paragraphs
The publication date
Whether the reader liked the book
questions.explain: "Effect on the reader" means the response the language deliberately provokes in the reader.

questions.q: Which sentence best uses 'show, not tell' to convey that a character is nervous?
options: She was very nervous about the exam.
Her hands trembled as she gripped the pencil, her eyes fixed on the clock.
She felt nervous and scared inside.
The girl was nervous because of the test.
questions.explain: Showing physical detail lets the reader infer the emotion rather than stating it outright.

questions.q: What is the reader most likely meant to FEEL from: "The orphan watched the other children open their gifts, his own hands empty"?
options: Sympathy for the orphan
Amusement
Boredom
Anger at the orphan
questions.explain: The image of the empty-handed orphan beside happy children is designed to evoke sympathy.

questions.q: Which paragraphing choice best helps a reader follow a piece of writing?
options: Beginning a new paragraph after every sentence
Never using paragraphs in formal writing
Starting a new paragraph for each new idea, time or place
Writing the whole piece as one long paragraph
questions.explain: Paragraphs are organised around shifts in idea, time, place or speaker to aid clarity.

questions.q: An extract begins in the middle of a chase with no introduction of who is running or why. This opening technique is designed to:
options: Explain the whole plot at once
Bore the reader before the action
End the story quickly
Plunge the reader straight into the action and create immediacy
questions.explain: Starting mid-action (in medias res) creates immediacy and draws the reader in at once.

questions.q: Which is the best way to adapt your writing for a young child as the audience?
options: Include dense statistics and technical jargon
Write in a formal, legalistic register
Use long, complex sentences and abstract vocabulary
Use simple, clear sentences, friendly tone and concrete vocabulary
questions.explain: Writing for young children needs simple sentences, a warm tone and accessible words.

questions.q: Which choice best describes the ATMOSPHERE in "Sunlight spilled across the kitchen and the kettle hummed a cheerful tune"?
options: Warm, homely and comforting
Threatening and cold
Chaotic and violent
Sad and lonely
questions.explain: Sunlight, a humming kettle and a "cheerful" tune build a warm, comforting atmosphere.

questions.q: "She laughed, but her eyes stayed cold." The contrast in this sentence most strongly suggests her laughter is:
options: Caused by a joke
Completely genuine
Insincere or hiding her true feelings
A sign of great joy
questions.explain: Warm laughter set against cold eyes implies the laughter is false and conceals real feeling.

questions.q: Which sentence uses the most ambitious, precise vocabulary?
options: The big house was really old and bad.
The house was very very scary.
The old house was scary and big.
The derelict mansion loomed, its decaying facade menacing the street.
questions.explain: 'Derelict', 'loomed', 'decaying' and 'menacing' are precise, ambitious word choices.

questions.q: What does 'planning' your writing before you start mainly help you to do?
options: Use up more time
Organise ideas logically and avoid drifting off task
Make the writing longer
Avoid using paragraphs
questions.explain: Planning structures ideas in advance so the writing stays coherent and on-task.
